original_question: Does the statement that the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem holds for any finite number of trees have the same reverse-mathematical strength as the statement that Milliken's theorem for colorings of finite strong trees holds?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem (6): Does "The Halpern-Läuchli Theorem holds for any finite number of trees" have the same strength as "Milliken’s Theorem for colorings of finite strong trees holds"?
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s official formulation. It correctly identifies the exact comparison the paper asks about: the reverse-mathematical relationship between the Halpern-Läuchli Theorem for any finite number of trees and Milliken’s theorem for colorings of finite strong trees.
missing_details: Make the base theory explicit: in this paper, reverse-mathematical comparison is meant over RCA0.
Identify the Milliken side precisely as statement (B) from the motivation: Milliken’s Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes.
Clarify that the Halpern-Läuchli side is the full "any finite number of trees" scheme, not the separate fixed-d questions from Problems (4) and (5).
Clarify that this asks about the full Milliken theorem for colorings of finite strong trees, not the separate fixed-height issue isolated in Problem (7).

If desired for context, note the known background direction recorded in the paper: in ZF, the Halpern-Läuchli statement implies the Milliken statement; the open reverse-mathematical issue is whether they are equivalent in strength.
refined_question: Over RCA0, is the statement that the Halpern-Läuchli Theorem holds for every finite number of trees equivalent in reverse-mathematical strength to Milliken’s Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes, i.e. Milliken’s theorem for colorings of finite strong trees?
justification: The draft is essentially a near-verbatim restatement of the paper’s official Problem (6), so that is the exact target to preserve. The only substantive additions needed to make it fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper are: first, to state the ambient reverse-mathematical base theory RCA0, which the paper makes explicit in the nearby umbrella question about equivalence of statements (A)-(D); and second, to identify the Milliken principle using the paper’s own contextual description in statement (B), namely Milliken’s Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes. The refined question should not drift into the fixed-d Halpern-Läuchli problems, the somewhere-dense-matrix variant, the height-specific Milliken fragments, or branching-degree comparisons, because those are split off as separate Problems (4), (5), (7), and (8).
